title: What we know about the Princess of Wales’ new documentary | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Catherine, Princess of Waleswill give an unusually personal and moving insight into life since hercancer diagnosisin a new documentary which follows her healing journey.

In the film, which premieres Sunday on the BBC for British viewers, cameras follow Kate, who revealed she was in remission in January 2025, as she takes on the National Three Peaks Challenge – one of the UK’s toughest mountain endurance tests – while reflecting on her experience along the way.

The mom-of-threecompleted the taskin June this year, scaling the highest peaks in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours to raise money for the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, which supports the hospital where she underwent treatment two years ago.

“This was an idea I had in the spring, not simply as a physical challenge but as a way of giving back to a community that holds great meaning for me and whose care and expertise are life-changing for so many people,” the 44-year-old princess said at a preview screening earlier this week.

In the film, Kate reflects on mortality and healing, meets others affected by cancer and is joined by her brother James, before receiving an emotional surprise from her children.

Here are some of the highlights:

Early in the 30-minute documentary, Kate describes how cancer goes beyond physical changes and forces a person to confront their own vulnerabilities.

“When you’re faced with your own mortality, you have to accept that life is not infinite,” she says, adding that the experience opens you up and “softens” your heart.

““Once you experience something like that, it’s very hard to go back to the person you were before. That’s when change can happen.””

— Catherine, Princess of Wales

For her, the challenge is a chance to explore what life and healing look like “beyond diagnosis, beyond treatment.”

Kate says conquering the Three Peaks is “a personal milestone” in her recovery, while also acknowledging that healing itself has no clear finish line.

“I don’t know what it’s going to be like. I don’t know if my body is physically strong enough yet,” she admits. “I’ve been training, but I don’t know if it’s enough. But this is really to understand that, you know, healing is a journey.”

She compares the challenge to “more of a pilgrimage” as she follows the same paths climbed by others on their own journeys of recovery.

Many cancer patients ring a bell to mark the end of treatment and the beginning of a new phase. But Kate never rang one, previously unaware of the tradition.

“I didn’t even know it was a thing,” she tells her brother James Middleton as the pair ascend Scafell Pike, England’s highest mountain and war memorial.

“Maybe this is your ringing of the bell,” he tells her. “I should’ve brought a bell with us.”

Kate has often spoken of her love of the natural world, hailing how it can support social and emotional wellbeing. She describes it as “my sanctuary and my refuge.”

“Even when I physically couldn’t get into nature, I imagined nature from my hospital bed,” she explains. “And now that I’m well enough, I feel a deep longing for all those spaces, for the ocean, for the trees, for the mountains.”

For the princess, the call of the wild feels almost spiritual. “I find that sense in nature more than anywhere, this feeling that you are part of something bigger and that something else holds you, even often when you can’t hold yourself.”

Kate recalls a “really dark” period in hospital when she was in and out of consciousness. What she remembers most is someone holding her hand.

“They weren’t talking to me. They weren’t trying to fix anything. They were just there,” she says. “You just need to be there. And that’s what love looks like.”

Her time in hospital also changed how she sees everyday life. “Something like cancer strips everything away,” she says.

““You do, in a way, lose yourself. I’m having to learn again to live life fully, finding joy in simple things.””

— Catherine, Princess of Wales

The experience, she says, taught her to slow down and be present in the moments that matter, a lesson she has also carried into parenting.

“We spend so much time doing and not being. And it’s a lesson that I’ve taken into being a parent too. Just being next to them, alongside them, is enough.”

At the top of the second mountain, Kate’s brother reveals he’s been in cahoots with her husband Prince William for a well-deserved reward, as James turns his phone to reveal video messages from her three children.

“Hello, Mummy. I really love you and I hope you do well going up the mountain. Remember, I’m always in your heart with you, and I love you very much,” eight-year-old Prince Louis can be heard saying.

Next, her eldest, Prince George, tells her to “keep going” and informs his mom that he’s tracking her and she looks “really strong.”

Princess Charlotte adds that the family is “so proud of you doing your walk and your challenges.” Moved by the messages, Kate says, “They gave me the reason to get out of hospital. They’re going to give me the reason to finish this challenge.”

And so she does. “Oh my gosh. Well done, body,” she tells herself after reaching the summit of the third and final mountain in Wales.

When she gets back to the bottom, Charlotte and Louis are seen leaping into their mom’s arms, a big grin on the princess’ face. She later appears overcome with emotion as she kisses George on the forehead and hugs him tight.

Kate says she set out to make a film that she hoped would encourage compassion. Her final message, which extends beyond her own journey, is that “whatever road you face, whatever challenge (lies) ahead, you are not alone. And that beauty and joy can still be found, even amidst the darkest of times.”

“Heal” airs in the United States on NBCUniversal on Monday, followed by Channel 9 in Australia on Tuesday and CTV and Noovo in Canada on December 7.
